metadata.title: AI and the Death of the 'Generic' Resume
metadata.register: Conversational-Balanced, first-person and reflective (matches the af_bella / @HumanitariansAI precedent set on this user's other reels, not the house Teardown register). Built on the ai-explainer chassis, not cli-explainer or deep-explainer's pantry/vox machinery — see note below.
metadata.note: User asked for a 'Deep Explainer' at exactly 4:00, based on the article 'AI and the Death of the Generic Resume.' The toolkit's actual deep-explainer skill targets 5-10 min (duration as an output, never a fixed target) and requires ~20-25% of body beats to be pantry stills (human-sourced or archival photos) with a two-gate pipeline that can block on unresolved sourcing. Both of those conflict with this request: a hard 4:00 target, and a topic with no natural archival-photo angle. Built instead on the ai-explainer chassis (Claude composer cold open -> body -> handoff -> outro), reusing the same all-self-generated-Manim/Remotion approach and af_bella/@HumanitariansAI branding already established on this user's other two reels, so the build has no external asset dependency and can be tuned to an exact duration via audio-first trimming. Functionally this delivers everything the user asked for (first-person, reflective, 4 clear movements + closing idea, 4:00) without the genre-mismatch risk of the heavier pipeline. CORRECTION (post-first-cut, per user request): the host self-introduction originally lived inside B00's cold-open narration; moved to a new dedicated B00B presenter-intro beat (Manim card: name + short lead-in) to match the presenter-intro pattern established on two-threads-one-week's B01 — B00 reverts to a plain ask-focused cold-open hook, consistent with ai-support-shift/two-threads-one-week's B00 convention.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask shown answered; the self-introduction now lives in the dedicated B00B presenter-intro beat, per the two-threads-one-week precedent
beats.narration_text: So I finally sat down and asked Claude to help me put this into words — because on my own, I couldn't quite land the phrasing.

props.command: claude "help me put into words a pattern I keep noticing every time I apply for a job"
props.segment: AI and the Death of the Generic Resume
output: a resume written by AI, read by AI

beats.role_note: presenter intro — 'Hi, I'm Agrima' self-introduction + a short lead-in to the topic, per user request; matches the presenter-intro precedent set on two-threads-one-week's B01 (ai-support-shift did not use a self-intro)
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. I want to talk about something that's been bugging me for a while now — a pattern I keep running into every single time I apply for a job.
beats.visual_intent: presenter card: name, then a short lead-in to the pattern this video is about — mirrors the two-threads-one-week B01 presenter-card treatment

beats.role_note: the application, sometimes personally recruited — SHOW
beats.narration_text: Here's the moment. You find a role, you apply — and sometimes it's not even cold. A recruiter found you first, messaged you personally, told you they thought you'd be a great fit. Maybe you'd been eyeing the company for months. Maybe the message just felt genuinely personal — not a template.
beats.visual_intent: two-step card sequence: recruiter reaches out -> you apply

beats.role_note: the instant automated rejection, zero explanation — SHOW
beats.narration_text: And then, minutes later — sometimes seconds — you get the rejection. Not even long enough for anyone to have opened the attachment, let alone read it. No feedback. No reason. Just a form email that already existed before your application finished uploading.
beats.visual_intent: timeline: Applied -> fast clock -> Rejected, footer states no feedback/no reason

beats.narration_text: It stops feeling like being turned down and starts feeling like being gaslit by the process itself — like you did something wrong, and nobody will tell you what it was. You start doubting the same resume that got you interviews just last year.
beats.visual_intent: typographic reveal: 'Gaslit by the process.' + subline

beats.role_note: recruiters who deny any auto-rejection — SHOW
beats.narration_text: So you start asking around, trying to understand what actually happened. And the answers contradict each other. Some recruiters insist, flatly, that no algorithm rejects anyone — every application gets read by a person. They point to their own process, their own team, as proof.
beats.visual_intent: quote card: 'No AI auto-rejects candidates. A person reads every application.' — some recruiters, when asked

beats.role_note: recruiters who admit automated pre-filtering — SHOW
beats.narration_text: Others admit it, more quietly: yes, software pre-screens for the hard requirements — visa sponsorship, location, years of experience — before a human ever sees the application at all. It's not malicious. It's just triage — too many applicants, not enough hours in anyone's day.
beats.visual_intent: quote card: 'We pre-screen for the hard requirements before a human sees it.' + checklist (Visa / Location / Years of experience)

beats.narration_text: And here's the part that actually gets to me: as the person applying, you have no way to know which one just happened to you. A human who skimmed and passed? Or code that never even parsed your name? There's no rejection letter that tells you which. You're left guessing at a system you can't see and can't appeal.
So I don't actually think this is a story about the resume dying. I think the real story is quieter than that, and a little stranger.
beats.visual_intent: minimal reframe card: 'Not a story about the resume dying.'

beats.narration_text: Not a person reading your story. Not even really you, anymore, doing the writing. Two systems, talking past you, about you.
beats.visual_intent: three-line typographic beat: Two systems. / Talking past you. / About you.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud AND discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time one of those instant rejections lands, try this: ask Claude to help you read between the lines — not to write you a fake resume, but to help you see it the way a filter might. What might it actually catch, and what's realistically just noise?

props.command:
claude "here's a job rejection I got less than a minute after
  applying. Help me think through what an automated filter
  might have caught — and what's probably just noise."
props.segment: AI and the Death of the Generic Resume

beats.role_note: OUTRO LAW — title restate, last beat
